title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
section: Late blight of potato and tomato
text: Late blight is caused by a water mould and spreads very fast in cool, cloudy, wet weather; it can destroy a field within days. It shows as pale green water-soaked patches on leaves that turn dark brown or black, often with white growth on the underside in humid weather. Act the same day you see it. Remove and destroy infected plants. Organic option: Bordeaux mixture or another copper product. Chemical option: mancozeb or chlorothalonil as a protective spray, or metalaxyl with mancozeb once the disease has appeared. Prevent it with certified seed, wide spacing, earthing up potato rows, and watering at the base in the morning. Do not grow tomato next to potato.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
section: Early blight of potato and tomato
text: Early blight is a fungal disease of older or stressed plants in warm weather. It shows as brown spots with rings like a target on the lower leaves, which then turn yellow and die. Remove infected lower leaves, mulch the soil and feed the crop well. Organic option: a copper product or a Trichoderma-based bio-fungicide. Chemical option: mancozeb or chlorothalonil at the first spots, repeated every 7 to 10 days.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
text: Powdery mildew is a fungal disease that looks like white powder on leaves and stems. It likes warm dry days with humid nights. Organic option: wettable sulphur, potassium bicarbonate or neem oil at the first sign. Space plants for air movement and avoid too much nitrogen.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
section: Bacterial spot of tomato and chilli
text: Bacterial spot shows as small dark greasy-looking spots on leaves and raised scabs on fruit. It arrives on infected seed or seedlings and spreads by rain splash and by handling wet plants. Use clean seed, rotate crops for two to three years, use drip irrigation and do not work in the crop when it is wet. Copper sprays slow it down.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
text: Leaf curl virus is spread by whiteflies; mosaic virus spreads by contact with hands, tools and infected seed. Leaves curl, yellow or show a light and dark green pattern and plants stay stunted. There is no cure for a plant that has a virus. Pull out infected plants and destroy them. Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps and neem oil, raise seedlings under insect-proof net, and wash hands and tools.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
text: Rusts show as small raised reddish-brown or orange pustules that rub off like powder. They spread by wind in cool, moist weather. Grow resistant varieties and sow on time. A fungicide such as propiconazole or mancozeb is used only when the infection is heavy early in the season.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
text: Spider mites are tiny pests, not a disease. Leaves show fine yellow speckles, turn bronze and have fine webbing underneath. They multiply in hot, dry, dusty weather. Wash the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water, spray neem oil, and keep the crop well watered. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the natural enemies of mites.

title: Common crop diseases and how to manage them
section: Why the same spray does not work on every disease
text: Fungicides work on fungal diseases, copper products help against bacterial diseases, and nothing cures a viral disease. That is why the disease must be identified before buying a product.

title: Where to get expert help
text: The Kisan Call Centre answers farmers' questions on the telephone in local languages. Call the toll-free number 1800-180-1551 from any mobile or landline. Agriculture graduates answer questions on crops, pests, diseases, weather, schemes and market prices, and pass difficult questions to subject experts.

title: Where to get expert help
text: A Krishi Vigyan Kendra is a farm science centre run under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). Most districts have one. Its scientists identify crop diseases and pests from a plant sample, test soil and water, demonstrate new varieties and methods on farmers' fields, and run free training. Take an affected plant, including leaves, stem and roots, in a paper bag when you visit.

title: Where to get expert help
section: When to ask an expert instead of relying on an app
text: Ask an expert when the app says its confidence is low, when the disease is spreading quickly through the field, when the first treatment has not worked after a week, when you are not sure which product or dose to use, and before using any product you have not used before. A photo-based app sees one leaf; an expert can examine the whole plant, the soil and the field.

title: Where to get expert help
text: Your block or district agriculture office has agriculture officers and extension workers who advise on seeds, fertiliser, schemes and subsidies and who visit fields. They are also the contact for crop loss reports and scheme applications.

title: Where to get expert help
text: Say which crop and variety you grow and how old the crop is, when you first saw the problem and how fast it is spreading, which part of the plant is affected, what the weather has been like, and what fertiliser and sprays you have already used. Photographs of the whole plant and of a close-up help.

title: Government schemes for farmers
text: PM-KISAN is an income support scheme of the Government of India. Eligible landholding farmer families receive 6,000 rupees a year, paid directly into the bank account in three instalments of 2,000 rupees. Registration needs Aadhaar, land records and a bank account linked to Aadhaar. e-KYC must be completed to keep receiving instalments. You can register and check your payment status on the PM-KISAN portal, through the PM-KISAN mobile app, or at a Common Service Centre.

title: Government schemes for farmers
section: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY, crop insurance)
text: PMFBY insures notified crops against loss from natural causes such as drought, flood, hailstorm, cyclone, pests and diseases. The farmer pays a small share of the premium: up to 2 percent of the sum insured for kharif food and oilseed crops, 1.5 percent for rabi food and oilseed crops, and 5 percent for annual commercial and horticultural crops. The government pays the rest. Enrol before the cut-off date for the season through your bank, a Common Service Centre, an insurance agent or the crop insurance portal or app.

title: Government schemes for farmers
section: Reporting a crop loss under PMFBY
text: For localised damage such as hailstorm, landslide or inundation, and for damage to harvested crop lying in the field, inform the insurance company, your bank or the agriculture office within 72 hours. You can report through the Crop Insurance app, the insurance company's toll-free number, or the bank or agriculture office. Keep photographs of the damage.

title: Government schemes for farmers
text: The Kisan Credit Card gives farmers short-term credit from banks for seed, fertiliser, pesticide and other cultivation costs, and also covers animal husbandry and fisheries. Crop loans up to 3 lakh rupees carry a subsidised interest rate, with a further reduction for farmers who repay on time. Apply at your bank branch, cooperative society or regional rural bank with identity proof, address proof and land records.

title: Government schemes for farmers
text: Under the Soil Health Card scheme, soil from your field is tested and you receive a card with fertiliser recommendations for your crops. Contact your agriculture office, soil testing laboratory or Krishi Vigyan Kendra to give a sample.

title: Government schemes for farmers
text: e-NAM is an online trading platform that connects mandis across India so farmers can see prices and sell produce to buyers in other markets. Register at your nearest e-NAM mandi with identity proof and bank details.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Integrated pest management (IPM) means using several methods together to keep pests and diseases below the level that causes real loss, and using chemical pesticides only when they are needed. It lowers cost, protects the natural enemies of pests and slows down resistance.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Use certified, disease-free seed and seedlings of varieties that resist the common diseases of your area. Treat seed before sowing. Rotate crops: do not grow the same crop, or crops of the same family such as tomato, potato, brinjal and chilli, on the same land season after season. Plough deep in summer to expose soil insects and disease spores to the sun. Keep the right spacing so air moves between plants and leaves dry quickly. Remove weeds, which shelter pests and diseases. Remove and destroy infected plants, fallen leaves and crop residue instead of leaving them in the field.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Too much nitrogen fertiliser makes soft, lush growth that attracts sucking pests and fungal diseases; apply fertiliser according to a soil test. Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves, and water in the morning so leaves are dry by night. Drip irrigation keeps leaves dry and reduces many leaf diseases. Avoid waterlogging, which causes root rot.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Walk through the field at least once a week and look at the underside of leaves, the growing tips and the stem base. Finding a problem early, when only a few plants are affected, makes it much easier to control. Remove the first infected leaves or plants by hand.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Yellow sticky traps catch whiteflies and aphids; blue sticky traps catch thrips. Pheromone traps attract and catch the moths of fruit borers and other caterpillars. Light traps catch many night-flying insects. Bird perches in the field help birds eat caterpillars. Protect helpful insects such as ladybird beetles, lacewings and spiders. Biological products include Trichoderma for soil and seed treatment against fungal diseases, Pseudomonas fluorescens against some bacterial and fungal diseases, and Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) against caterpillars.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
text: Neem seed kernel extract and neem oil sprays reduce sucking pests and small caterpillars and are safe for most helpful insects. Spray in the evening and cover the underside of the leaves. These sprays work best when pest numbers are still low.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
section: Chemical control as the last step
text: Use a chemical pesticide only when the pest or disease has crossed the level where it causes economic loss. Choose a product approved for that crop and problem, use the label dose, and do not repeat the same chemical group again and again; rotating groups slows resistance. Follow the waiting period before harvest.

title: Integrated pest and disease management
section: Fungal, bacterial and viral diseases are treated differently
text: Fungal diseases such as blights, leaf spots, rusts and mildews can be controlled with fungicides if treated early. Bacterial diseases such as bacterial spot are managed mainly with clean seed, copper sprays and keeping leaves dry. Viral diseases such as leaf curl and mosaic have no cure: remove infected plants and control the insects that spread the virus, such as whiteflies and aphids.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Neem seed kernel extract is a spray made from crushed neem seed kernels soaked overnight in water and filtered. It discourages sucking pests such as aphids, whiteflies and jassids and small caterpillars, and is gentle on helpful insects. A little soap is added so the spray sticks to the leaves. Spray in the evening and wet the underside of the leaves. It works best when pest numbers are still low and needs repeating after rain.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Neem oil mixed with water and a little soap is used against sucking pests, mites and powdery mildew. Shake well, spray in the evening, and test on a few plants first because strong mixtures can burn tender leaves.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Jeevamrut is a fermented liquid made from cow dung, cow urine, jaggery, pulse flour, a handful of soil and water. It is applied to the soil with irrigation water or sprayed in diluted form to increase helpful soil microbes. It is a soil conditioner, not a pesticide.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Bordeaux mixture is a traditional fungicide made from copper sulphate and lime in water. It protects against blights, leaf spots and downy mildew. It must be prepared fresh, with the two solutions made separately in non-metal containers and then combined. Too much copper can burn leaves, so follow the proportions recommended by your KVK.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Trichoderma is a helpful fungus sold as a powder. It is mixed with seed before sowing or with farmyard manure and applied to the soil to protect roots from wilt and root rot fungi. Do not mix it with chemical fungicides.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Compost is made by rotting crop residue, weeds and dung in a heap or pit kept moist and turned every few weeks. Vermicompost is made by earthworms from partly rotted organic waste and is richer in nutrients. Both improve soil structure, water holding and soil life.

title: Organic and low-cost inputs
text: Covering the soil around plants with dry leaves, straw or crop residue keeps moisture in, keeps weeds down and stops soil with disease spores from splashing onto the lower leaves.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Identify the pest or disease first. Spraying the wrong product wastes money and can harm the crop. Buy only from a licensed dealer and ask for a bill. Check that the pack is sealed, has a label in a language you can read, and has not passed its expiry date. Buy only the amount needed for this season.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: The label and leaflet tell you the crop and pest the product is approved for, the dose per acre or per litre of water, how many days to wait between the last spray and harvest (the waiting period or pre-harvest interval), and first aid. The coloured triangle on the label shows how poisonous the product is: red is extremely toxic, yellow is highly toxic, blue is moderately toxic and green is slightly toxic. Prefer blue or green label products when they are effective.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Use exactly the dose written on the label. A higher dose does not work better; it burns the crop, leaves more residue on the produce and makes pests resistant. Measure with a measuring cap, not by guess. Mix in a bucket with a stick, never with bare hands. Do not mix two products together unless the label or an agriculture officer says they can be mixed.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Wear full sleeves, long trousers, shoes, gloves, a mask or cloth over the nose and mouth, and eye protection. Do not eat, drink, smoke or chew tobacco while spraying. Spray with the wind at your back so the mist blows away from you. Do not blow into a blocked nozzle with your mouth; clean it with a thin wire or water. Keep children and animals away from the field.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Spray in the early morning or late afternoon, when the air is calm and cool. Do not spray in strong wind, in the hot midday sun, or when rain is expected in the next few hours, because rain washes the product off before it works. Avoid spraying when the crop is flowering and bees are active; if you must, spray in the evening after bees have returned to the hive.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Wash the sprayer away from wells, ponds and canals. Wash your hands, face and body with soap, and wash the clothes you wore separately. Put up a sign or tell family and workers not to enter the field for the time stated on the label. Do not harvest or sell the crop before the waiting period on the label has passed.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Keep pesticides in their original containers, locked, away from food, animal feed and children. Never store them in drinking water bottles or food containers. Rinse empty containers three times, pour the rinse water into the spray tank, then puncture and crush the containers so they cannot be reused. Do not burn them or throw them into water.

title: Safe use of pesticides
text: Signs include headache, dizziness, vomiting, heavy sweating, blurred vision, stomach pain and difficulty breathing. Move the person to fresh air, remove contaminated clothes and wash the skin with plenty of soap and water. If the product went into the eyes, wash them with clean water for 15 minutes. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person. Take the person to a doctor immediately and carry the pesticide container or label with you.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
section: What the Soil Health Card is
text: The Soil Health Card is a printed report given to farmers under a Government of India scheme. A soil sample from your field is tested in a laboratory and the card shows the status of the soil and recommends how much fertiliser and manure to apply for different crops. Using it helps you avoid spending on fertiliser the soil does not need.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
text: The card reports major nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K). It reports sulphur, and micronutrients such as zinc, iron, copper, manganese and boron. It also reports soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is), electrical conductivity (salt level) and organic carbon (a measure of organic matter). Each value is rated, usually as low, medium or high, with a fertiliser recommendation.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
section: How to take a soil sample
text: Take the sample after harvest and before applying fertiliser or manure. Do not sample near bunds, trees, manure heaps or wet spots. In each field, dig a V-shaped cut about 15 cm deep at 8 to 10 spots spread across the field in a zigzag, and take a thin slice of soil from each. Mix all the slices on a clean cloth, remove stones and roots, and keep about half a kilogram. Dry it in the shade, put it in a clean cloth or plastic bag with your name, village, survey number and the crop you plan to grow, and give it to the soil testing laboratory, agriculture office or Krishi Vigyan Kendra.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
text: A pH of about 6.5 to 7.5 suits most crops. Below 6 the soil is acidic; liming materials are used to correct it. Above 8.5 the soil is alkaline; gypsum and organic matter are commonly used. Do not apply lime or gypsum without a soil test recommendation.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
section: What N, P and K do for the plant
text: Nitrogen gives green, leafy growth; a shortage shows as pale yellow older leaves and stunted plants. Phosphorus builds roots and helps flowering and seed formation; a shortage shows as dark or purplish leaves and poor root growth. Potassium strengthens the plant against disease, drought and lodging and improves grain and fruit quality; a shortage shows as yellowing and drying along the edges of older leaves.

title: Soil health and the Soil Health Card
text: Add farmyard manure, compost or vermicompost every year. Grow a green manure crop such as dhaincha or sunn hemp and plough it in before flowering. Include a pulse crop in the rotation, because pulses fix nitrogen from the air. Return crop residue to the soil instead of burning it; burning destroys organic matter and helpful soil life. Use biofertilisers such as Rhizobium for pulses and Azotobacter or phosphate solubilising bacteria for other crops. Apply chemical fertiliser in the amount the soil test recommends, in split doses.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Irrigate at the stages when a shortage of water costs the most yield: for most crops these are establishment, flowering and grain or fruit filling. Check soil moisture by pressing a handful of soil from root depth; if it does not hold together, the crop needs water. Irrigate in the morning or evening to reduce evaporation.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Drip irrigation delivers water to the root zone and can save a large share of the water used in flood irrigation; it also keeps leaves dry, which reduces leaf diseases. Sprinklers suit closely sown crops. Mulching reduces evaporation. Level the field so water spreads evenly. Subsidy for drip and sprinkler systems is available under the Per Drop More Crop component of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana; ask your agriculture or horticulture office.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Waterlogging starves roots of air and causes root rot and wilting. Make drainage channels before the monsoon and grow vegetables on raised beds in heavy rainfall areas.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Many fungal diseases spread when leaves stay wet for long periods. Several days of cloudy, humid or rainy weather are a warning to inspect the crop closely, especially potato and tomato for late blight. Hot, dry weather favours mites and sucking pests.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Do not spray when rain is expected within a few hours, when the wind is strong, or in the midday heat. The best time is a calm early morning or late afternoon.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: The India Meteorological Department issues district-level agromet advisories twice a week with a five-day forecast and crop advice. They are available on the Meghdoot mobile app and through Krishi Vigyan Kendras. The Damini app gives lightning warnings.

title: Water, irrigation and weather
text: Before heavy rain, harvest mature produce, clear drainage channels and postpone fertiliser and pesticide application. Before a heat wave, give light, frequent irrigation and mulch the soil. Before frost, irrigate lightly in the evening, because moist soil holds more heat.
